requirement: A `{req}` opening fence MAY contain four or more colons. Habeas MUST accept opening fences of any length of at least three colons. A colon-only line with fewer colons than the opener MUST remain inside the requirement body, allowing a nested colon directive. A closing fence outside a fenced code example with at least as many colons as the opener MUST end the body.
rationale:
structural: `requirements.ci.fence_lengths` states only observable parsing behavior. Each clause is about what Habeas accepts or how it delimits a requirement body:
- "A `{req}` opening fence MAY contain four or more colons." This is optional and imposes nothing to check.
- "Habeas MUST accept opening fences of any length of at least three colons." This is about which inputs are accepted.
- "A colon-only line with fewer colons than the opener MUST remain inside the requirement body, allowing a nested colon directive." This is about where the body boundary falls.
- "A closing fence outside a fenced code example with at least as many colons as the opener MUST end the body." This is also about where the body boundary falls.

The text names no library, algorithm, signature, type, field, or delegation through a named interface. A different parser would give the same results. For example, a hand-written line scanner, a regex, or a Markdown-library tokenizer could each implement these rules with identical results. None of those choices would violate any clause, so how the parser is built is discretionary. No implementation roots were supplied, and none are needed. Tests supply evidence for the behavioral obligations.

behavioral: The reviewed tests cover every behavioral obligation in `requirements.ci.fence_lengths`.

- **Openers of any length of at least three colons.** `src/evidence.rs#mod[tests]/fn[validates_four_or_more_colon_fences_and_longer_closers]` uses openers of 4 and 7 colons, and `src/lib.rs#mod[tests]/fn[a_longer_colon_fence_contains_a_shorter_nested_directive]` uses a 4-colon opener. Both assert that exactly one requirement is parsed. The 3-colon opener is covered by `src/evidence.rs#mod[tests]/fn[colon_requirement_span_includes_markdown_and_excludes_following_text]`. `src/fenced.rs#mod[tests]/fn[markdown_fences_close_with_enough_colons_and_skip_code]` also covers a 4-colon opener. `src/evidence.rs#mod[tests]/fn[example_bodies_keep_nested_markdown_and_trim_outer_whitespace]` covers 4- and 6-colon `{example}` openers.
- **A colon-only line with fewer colons than the opener stays in the body.** The same tests put a nested `:::{note}...:::` inside 4-colon and 7-colon fences. They assert that the body, including the nested closer and the text after it, is retained and that no error is reported. The `markdown_fences_close_with_enough_colons_and_skip_code` test asserts the exact body slice. It includes `"::: trailing\n    :::\n"` for a 3-colon opener and `"outer\n:::{impl} c.d\ninner\n:::\n"` for a 4-colon opener.
- **A closer with at least as many colons ends the body.** Equal (4/4) and longer (4/5, 7/8, and 6/7 for examples) closers are tested. The text after the closer ("Outside the requirement.", "Outside.", "Text after the example.") is excluded. This is asserted through the report, the body ranges and `blocks[0].end`, and the example text equality. `markdown_fences_close_with_enough_colons_and_skip_code` also checks that `   :::::  ` closes a 3-colon opener.
- **A closer inside a fenced code example does not end the body.** `colon_requirement_span_includes_markdown_and_excludes_following_text` has `:::` inside a ```text block, and the full body is expected to be preserved. `markdown_fences_close_with_enough_colons_and_skip_code` and the example-body test have `:::{cite}` and `:::{example}` lines inside code fences. They assert that these lines are skipped, and in the fenced test that they are treated as ordinary text in plain mode.

I found no requirement-violating behavior that these assertions would accept.
